title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 10 Nov 2026]
Title:Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a model by up to 45 places.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper finds arena-style preference leaderboards can be gamed via strategic voting, prompting, and nomination, shifting models by up to 45 ranks.
report.background: Arena-style leaderboards have become a default signal for comparing large language models. They sample anonymous pairwise battles on user-submitted prompts, then aggregate wins and losses with the Bradley-Terry model into a global ranking. These rankings influence research claims, procurement decisions, investor narratives, and public perception. Because many arenas allow open prompting, open voting, and open model submission, they create incentives for providers to manipulate outcomes rather than improve models. Earlier evaluation concerns focused on benchmark contamination and overfitting to test sets; preference-based arenas were often treated as more realistic because humans or users supply prompts and compare outputs. This paper tests that assumption by modeling adversarial behavior in the open arena pipeline. It shows that small, strategic actions can compound into large rank changes, and it argues the vulnerability is structural for any Bradley-Terry-based preference evaluation with open participation. The findings arrive as model vendors increasingly cite leaderboard position in marketing and as enterprises look for trustworthy third-party evaluation.
key_points: Strategic voting lets an unscrupulous provider or coordinated group cast votes that improve a target model's Bradley-Terry score. The paper finds that even votes on irrelevant models can reshape the ranking, because every pairwise outcome affects the fitted model strengths. This turns open voting into an attack surface rather than a neutral measurement channel.

Strategic prompting means choosing prompts that disproportionately favor a target model. In an open arena, providers can submit many comparisons designed to showcase strengths or expose competitor weaknesses. The sampled prompt distribution then no longer reflects real user traffic, so the aggregate ranking can drift even if individual votes are honest.

Strategic nomination involves inserting irrelevant models into the arena. Adding weak or poorly matched candidates changes the pairwise comparison graph and the Bradley-Terry fit, which can lift a target model's relative rank. This is especially concerning because model submission is often lightly controlled and the inserted models need not be serious competitors.

The effects are large. Each manipulation strategy can move a model by roughly 15 to 20 places, and combined attacks can shift it by up to 45 places. The authors demonstrate this on public leaderboard data and note the issue generalizes to any preference-based evaluation using Bradley-Terry with open prompting, voting, or model submission.

The paper describes safeguards for each attack, including more robust vote aggregation, prompt auditing, restrictions on model submission, anomaly detection, and statistical checks. It does not propose a single fix; instead it argues leaderboard operators must treat preference data as adversarial and design evaluation pipelines with manipulation resistance in mind.
report.impact: The finding undermines the assumption that arena leaderboards are neutral ground truth. For the AI industry, leaderboard position is a marketing and procurement signal, so manipulation risk can distort vendor competition and investment. For developers, it means model selection should combine arena results with controlled benchmarks, private evals, and task-specific testing; open preference data should be audited, not trusted blindly. For regular users, a higher rank may not reflect better real-world performance, especially when open prompting and voting invite gaming. The broader lesson is that evaluation is an adversarial problem: as models converge, incentives to game rankings grow, and leaderboard operators will need transparency, robust statistics, and independent auditing to preserve trust.
report.tools: Follow the public data and methods behind Chatbot Arena/LMArena, plus open-source arena infrastructure such as FastChat. For controlled evaluation, watch lm-evaluation-harness and HELM. For ranking robustness, examine Bradley-Terry and OpenSkill implementations, vote-weighting methods, and anomaly-detection tooling for prompt and vote distributions. Leaderboard operators should publish submission and voting audits; researchers can reproduce attacks on public leaderboard dumps to test safeguards.
